The SF host the DEN as favorites of 2.5, with the total set at 46.5 — a market that implies a SF 24–22 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 26% of its snaps with SF in front, 39% within one score, and 34% with SF chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This is a coin-flip script. With only 2.5 points separating them, neither team projects to spend much time in a blowout state — most of the game lives in the 'close' bucket, where play-calling stays balanced and usage tracks each player's established role rather than being distorted by score. In tight games the stars on both sides see their normal, dependable workloads, and there is less garbage-time leakage to backups.

The Key Matchups

Tough sledding for Christian McCaffrey — DEN are stingy against the run (102 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Courtland Sutton faces a tough cover — SF hold WR1s to just 51 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A middling 46 total — no strong lean either way; the value is in the individual matchups above, not the game environment.

SF — a run-heavy offense

SF are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 40% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

Christian McCaffrey (16 carries, 76 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Mike Evans projects for 7 targets and 60 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, George Kittle (TE, 6 targets, 64 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

DEN — a balanced offense

DEN are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (43% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

J.K. Dobbins (13 carries, 62 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Courtland Sutton projects for 6 targets and 50 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Evan Engram (TE, 3 targets, 21 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 2-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.
